3.1.1.examLens: Read a multi-vari chart and name the dominant source of variation. It is a narrowing tool, used before any formal statistical test.

worked.question: A multi-vari chart for a machined part shows readings within each piece differ by about 0.002, the five pieces in each hourly sample average within about 0.003 of each other, but the hourly averages move up and down by about 0.020 over the day. Which family dominates, and where would you look first?
worked.solution: Time-to-time dominates (0.020 versus 0.003 and 0.002). Look at what changes through the day: tool wear, temperature, shift or operator changes, material lots, or setup drift.

3.1.2.examLens: Match a situation to the right distribution, know the formulas for the binomial and Poisson, and know which test statistics come from which distribution.

worked.question: Match each to a distribution: (a) scratches on a car panel; (b) defective units in a sample of 20; (c) time between machine breakdowns; (d) right-skewed repair times that cannot be negative; (e) drawing 5 units from a lot of 50 without replacement. Then compute the Poisson probability of exactly 2 scratches if the average is 3.

3.1.1.a.title: Purpose
3.1.1.a.html: A multi-vari study finds which family of variation is largest, so the team knows where to look. It is graphical and uses a structured sampling plan, not a hypothesis test. Use it early in Analyze, before you spend effort testing individual causes.

3.1.1.b.title: The three families
3.1.1.b.html:
• Within-piece (positional): variation across a single unit. Example: the diameter at different positions along one shaft.
  • Piece-to-piece: variation between units made close together in time. Example: five consecutive shafts.
  • Time-to-time (temporal): variation between time periods. Example: morning versus afternoon, one day versus the next, one shift versus another.

3.1.1.c.title: How it is done
3.1.1.c.html:
1. Pick a sampling interval (for example every hour).
  2. At each interval, take several consecutive pieces.
  3. Measure each piece at several positions.
  4. Plot every reading on a chart with time on the horizontal axis, joining the piece averages and the time-period averages.
  5. Compare the size of the three kinds of variation visually.

3.1.1.d.title: The largest family points to the Red X
3.1.1.d.html:
The family with the biggest swing tells you where the key cause lives.

  • Mostly within-piece: look at things that act on one piece (fixture, clamping, tool geometry).
  • Mostly piece-to-piece: look at things that change from unit to unit (material, setup repeatability).
  • Mostly time-to-time: look at things that change over time (tool wear, shift, ambient temperature, material lot).

3.1.1.e.title: Variance components
3.1.1.e.html:
Extension. A nested ANOVA puts numbers on the same idea by splitting total variance into components.
Example: positional σ = 0.002, piece-to-piece σ = 0.003, time-to-time σ = 0.010. Variances: 0.000004, 0.000009, 0.0001. Total = 0.000113. Time-to-time share = 0.0001 ÷ 0.000113 = 88%.

3.1.1.f.title: Name the dominant source
3.1.1.f.html: On a chart, find which swing is widest: the spread inside each cluster of readings (within-piece), the spread between pieces in a cluster (piece-to-piece), or the movement of the cluster averages over time (time-to-time).

3.1.2.a.title: Continuous distributions
3.1.2.a.html:
• Normal: symmetric bell curve; most measurements of a stable process.
  • Lognormal: positively skewed, cannot go below zero (repair times, some cycle times).
  • Weibull: flexible shape; time to failure.
  • Exponential: time between random events.
  • Uniform: every value in a range equally likely.

3.1.2.b.title: Discrete distributions
3.1.2.b.html:
• Binomial: counts of pass/fail results (defectives) in a fixed number of trials.
  • Poisson: counts of defects over a fixed amount of opportunity.
  • Hypergeometric: like the binomial, but sampling without replacement from a small population.

3.1.2.c.title: Binomial
3.1.2.c.html:
P(x) = nCx · pˣ · (1 − p)ⁿ⁻ˣ. Mean = np. Standard deviation = √[np(1 − p)].
Example: n = 10, p = 0.1. P(2 defectives) = 45 × 0.01 × 0.9⁸ = 45 × 0.01 × 0.4305 = 0.194. Mean = 1.

3.1.2.d.title: Poisson
3.1.2.d.html:
P(x) = e^(−λ) · λˣ ÷ x!. Mean = variance = λ.
Example: λ = 3 defects per unit. P(0) = e⁻³ = 0.0498. P(1) = 3e⁻³ = 0.1494, so P(1 or fewer) = 0.199.

3.1.2.e.title: Exponential
3.1.2.e.html:
Models the time between events when events occur at a constant average rate. It is memoryless: the chance of an event in the next hour does not depend on how long you have already waited. P(T beyond t) = e^(−t ÷ mean).
Example: mean time between failures is 50 hours. P(no failure for 100 hours) = e⁻² = 0.135.

3.1.2.f.title: Sampling distributions
3.1.2.f.html:
These describe test statistics.

  • t: like the normal but with heavier tails; depends on degrees of freedom and approaches the normal as df grows. Used for means when σ is estimated.
  • Chi-square (χ²): positive and skewed; used for variances and contingency tables.
  • F: a ratio of two variances; used for comparing variances and in ANOVA.

3.1.2.g.title: Typical uses
3.1.2.g.html: Time-to-failure data often follow Weibull or exponential. Positively skewed data bounded at zero often follow lognormal.

3.1.2.h.title: Approximations
3.1.2.h.html: Extension. The Poisson approximates the binomial when p is small and n is large. The normal approximates the binomial when both np and n(1 − p) are at least 5 (some use 10). Treat these as exam rules of thumb.

3.1.2.i.title: Match the scenario
3.1.2.i.html: Defects on a unit = Poisson. Defective units in a sample = binomial. Time between breakdowns = exponential. Right-skewed, strictly positive times = lognormal or Weibull.

3.1.2.j.title: Assumptions behind each
3.1.2.j.html:
• Binomial: a fixed number of trials, each independent, with the same probability of a defective.
  • Poisson: counts over a fixed exposure (area, time, unit) at a constant average rate.
  • Exponential: time between events that occur at a constant rate.
  • Weibull: flexible failure behavior, controlled by a shape parameter.

3.1.2.k.title: Which distribution goes with which data
3.1.2.k.html: Defectives, binomial. Defects, Poisson. Continuous measurements, normal, lognormal, or Weibull. The t, F, and χ² are not data distributions. They are the sampling distributions behind the tests in 3.3 to 3.5.

3.1.2.l.title: Weibull shape and the hypergeometric
3.1.2.l.html: Extension. Weibull shape β: below 1 means early failures, equal to 1 is random failures (exponential), above 1 means wear-out. The hypergeometric applies when you sample without replacement from a small population, roughly when the sample is about 5% of the population or more.

3.1.1-1.stem: A multi-vari chart for a machined part shows readings within each piece differing by about 0.001, the five pieces in each hourly sample differing by about 0.002, and the hourly averages moving up and down by about 0.015 over the day. Where should the team look first?

options.html: At the measurement positions on each piece
At unit-to-unit differences in the setup
At things that change through the day, such as tool wear, temperature, or shift changes

3.1.1-1.explanation: Time-to-time variation (0.015) is far larger than piece-to-piece (0.002) or within-piece (0.001), so the key cause is something that changes over time.

3.1.1-2.stem: A multi-vari study is a formal hypothesis test that produces a p-value.
3.1.1-2.explanation: It is a graphical tool for narrowing down which family of variation is largest. It is used before formal testing.

3.1.1-3.stem: Differences between the morning shift and the afternoon shift are an example of which family of variation?
3.1.1-3.explanation: Differences between time periods, such as shifts or days, are time-to-time (temporal) variation.

3.1.1-4.stem: A multi-vari study shows most of the variation is within each piece (positional). Which cause is most likely to be investigated first?

options.html: Differences between operators on different shifts
Fixture clamping or tool geometry that acts on a single piece
Changes in raw material lots between days

3.1.1-4.explanation: Variation across a single piece points to factors acting on that piece, such as fixturing and tooling.

3.1.2-1.stem: Which distribution is the best model for the number of scratches on a painted panel?
3.1.2-1.explanation: Counts of defects over a fixed area or unit follow the Poisson pattern.

3.1.2-2.stem: A process has a 20% defective rate. In a sample of 5 units, what is the probability that exactly 2 are defective?

3.1.2-3.stem: Defects occur on a unit at an average of 2 per unit. What is the probability that a unit has no defects?

3.1.2-4.stem: The mean time between machine failures is 40 hours, and failures follow an exponential distribution. What is the probability that the machine runs more than 80 hours without a failure?

3.1.2-5.explanation: Normal and Weibull model measured values. Binomial and Poisson are discrete.

3.1.2-6.stem: Which sampling distribution is used when comparing two variances?
3.1.2-6.explanation: The ratio of two variances follows an F distribution.

3.1.2-7.stem: Which assumption is required for the binomial distribution?

options.html: A fixed number of independent trials, each with the same probability of a defective
The mean must equal the variance

3.1.2-7.explanation: Binomial counts successes in a fixed number of independent trials with constant probability. Mean equal to variance is a Poisson property.

3.1.2-8.stem: A Weibull analysis of failure data gives a shape parameter well above 1. What does this indicate?
3.1.2-8.explanation: A shape below 1 means early failures, equal to 1 means random failures (exponential), and above 1 means wear-out.
